To investigate the computational effectiveness of ab initio molecular dynamics simulations for biomolecules, the alanine dipeptide model was used and simulated over multiple methods (TD-DFT, ADMM, TPA, second-order non-linear response theory) using small basis sets (RHF, UHF). The results show that the linear response time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) has significant errors compared to higher-level approaches, while the time-dependent second-order non-linear response theory (TPA) and adaptive multi-pole method (ADMM) demonstrated more accuracy. However, the zero-knowledge algorithm could not achieve the desired property. The study finds that the coupled-cluster with single and double excitations using an active space (CC2-AS) using a large basis set shows the best performance, but is computationally expensive. Ultimately, the study recommends using the TPA/ADMM combination with a small basis set for ab initio MD simulations. To further improve the method, it is suggested that TPA calculations be optimized, and that larger basis sets be employed to be compatible with CC2-AS. Additionally, it is recommended that adiabatic MD simulations be conducted using higher-level theories (CC2-AS, TPA/ADMM) to verify the simulation results. Lastly, it is suggested that the zero-knowledge algorithm be re-implemented to achieve the desired property.

Unlike the conventional single-user approach, our strategy utilizes multiple waves to serve multiple users simultaneously. Additionally, our wideband waveforming technique outperforms a single-user strategy by at least an order of magnitude in terms of throughput and meets or exceeds the limits of our laboratory equipment in throughput fairness and total throughput.

This study investigates the implications of employing underrepresented loss functions in the development of artificial intelligence models. Specifically, we examine the performance of models utilizing KL Divergence as a loss function for category imbalanced classification, which is a common issue in real-world data sets. Although KL Divergence is an unbalanced loss function, capable of producing impressive results in balanced data sets, we observe significant imbalances between classes in real-world data. As a result, we conduct an unbalanced classification experiment using a deeply learned feature extraction model, and analyze the efficacy of different loss functions, including KL Divergence, between class-imbalanced data sets. Our findings reveal that KL Divergence performs poorly compared to other loss functions like Focal Loss and Asymmetric Loss, which are more commonly used with class-imbalanced data sets. However, we also find that KL Divergence produces better results when combining multiple classes into a single class, which we term a highly imbalanced data set. To address this issue, we propose an adaptive KL Divergence loss function that adjusts to the ratio of class instances, demonstrating improved accuracy compared to other loss functions with both moderately and highly imbalanced data sets. Our code is available on GitHub, and our findings provide valuable insights for developing loss functions for use with class-imbalanced data sets.

Neural models have been highly effective in various language tasks but often require an vast amount of manually classified data. If-then relationships, represented as if $P$ then $Q$, are no exception, with most models trained on flat categories or no structure at all. In contrast, many domains like biology and medicine have intricately structured relationships that could be more accurately predicted with hierarchical relationships. Our study introduces a new approach where models learn if-then relationships based on a pre-defined hierarchy of cause and effect categories. We demonstrate that neural models perform better when trained with hierarchy-structured data and establish a new benchmark consisting of highly relevant relationships. Our results show that strong models like BERT and RoBERTa achieve the best results when all condition and effect categories are known in advance. However, we also observe that models perform significantly better when the hierarchy is more defined and less deep, leading to the recommendation of using two levels of hierarchy at most. Our findings provide valuable insights into the development of if-then relationship classification models and make a strong case for the use of hierarchy-structured data. We further introduce a new dataset consisting of highly relevant relationships in the field of computer vision and auditation that exceeds the performance of the current benchmark. Our code and dataset are available for download on GitHub.

Unlike the standard model, we propose a scenario where the contextual distribution is unknown and must be learned from the environment. This distribution's knowledge may not always be directly actionable, leading to the idea of "advocating" for desirable context combinations by taking actions that result in informative feedback. Under these conditions, we found that freeze-out of carbon monoxide occurs earlier than expected, reducing gas cooling capacity further. As a result, we determine that actual cooling efficiencies in these systems often fall short of the theoretical maximum by a factor of two to three. These findings provide critical insights for understanding the full range of cooling efficiencies in protoplanetary disk systems and their role in shaping planetary formation scenarios. Moreover, we propose that dust grain growth and settling may serve as a more effective cooling inhibitor in these systems than previously thought, leaving a gap in our model that requires further investigation. To accurately calculate cooling efficiencies, we recommend using dust temperature data from infrared observations or developing more precise ALMA observation protocols. Single-particle entanglement is a key component of non-local phenomena such as quantum steering and Bell non-locality. However, due to its lack of correlation with two-particle states, single-particle entanglement is ineffective in generating these effects. Here we show that in macroscopic quantum systems like Bose-Einstein condensates, non-locality can arise from single-particle entanglement, counterintuitive as that may seem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that even in situations where two-particle correlations are strongly influenced by three-body interactions, single-particle entanglement remains the dominant source of non-locality. Our findings provide a new perspective on the distribution of non-locality within complex quantum systems. Additionally, we derive a general entanglement monotone that captures the inherent connection between single-particle entanglement and non-locality, and apply it to investigate the non-locality of condensates in a harmonic trap following a sudden interaction switch. Lastly, we outline the practical limitations of single-particle entanglement-based non-locality through an analysis of the maximum achievable Fain-Sandin entanglement as a function of particle number. Our research paves the way for exploring the non-locality of single-particle entanglement in complex quantum systems and investigates the feasibility of detecting it through two-particle correlations. Moreover, we provide a framework for optimizing three-body interactions to enhance non-locality and provide a perspective on its relation to other entanglement measures such as concurrence and log-negativity.

Hypothesis selection is a crucial process in scientific inquiry, where limited data forces choices between alternative theories or models. Ranks, derived from the expected utility of each hypothesis, play a key role in decision-making during this process. Previously, we introduced the "Hypothesis Selection with Utility from Ranks" problem, aiming to efficiently determine the hypothesis yielding the highest utility when utility functions are unknown and must be estimated from limited data. In this study, we address the analogous problem of identifying the top-k hypotheses, which are the highest utility rankings. We provide new insights and bounds for this problem, exploring the connection between hypothesis utility and ranks when utility estimation is subject to error. Furthermore, we explore the scenario where multiple utility estimation methods are available and select the most suitable approach. All proposed solutions, along with existing approaches, will be evaluated and compared through comprehensive theoretical analyses, solving for the optimal utility threshold, rejecting false positives, and identifying the top-k hypotheses. Our results contribute to the understanding of hypothesis selection with utility from ranks and provide actionable advice for data collection strategies. Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of our findings to various real-world scenarios, including climate model evaluation, molecular structure prediction, and statistical inference. All algorithm descriptions, along with the code, are available on Bitbucket. All theoretical analyses were conducted using Mathematica, with the symbol manipulation system fully integrated into the code. The code and data used for real-world examples are available on GitHub. All experiments were performed on a Linux-based system with an Intel Xeon Gold 6130 processor, 256 GB RAM, and an NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU. Our findings offer practical guidance for the hypothesis selection with utility from ranks, exploring multiple real-world applications and presenting actionable advice for data collection strategies.

While a full hydrodynamic simulation would provide more accurate results, the $N$-body approach is practical for large-scale simulations. To address this limitation, a new model that only considers density fluctuations is introduced and combined with an existing model that accounts for velocity dispersions. Using a variety of simulation datasets with different amplitudes of initial scalar perturbations, the model shows consistent predictions of halo masses across multiple orders of magnitude, demonstrating its potential to fill the gap between linear and non-linear hydrodynamic models. Consequently, the standard model of cosmological evolution (LCDM) is verified up to nonlinear hydrodynamic scales, and the model's ability to predict halo masses through a variety of parameter studies is demonstrated. The model's performance is verified against multiple hydrodynamic simulation datasets, with the hydrodynamic model extending the reach of $N$-body simulations by multiple orders of magnitude.
